header.title: Integrations
header.description: Copy-paste recipes for plugging ProxMenux Monitor into the dashboards and tools your homelab already uses — Homepage, Home Assistant, Grafana via Prometheus, Uptime Kuma. Each recipe shows the exact config the receiving tool expects, the Monitor endpoint it talks to, and the auth header pattern that holds it together.

intro.title: What you can build from this page
intro.body: Every recipe below is ready to copy into your tool of choice. The API endpoints used here are documented in the <link>API Reference</link> — this page is the "here's how to actually use them in Homepage / Home Assistant / Grafana" companion. Screenshots show the real output you'll see once the recipe is in place.

auth.heading: Authentication: the one thing every recipe needs
auth.intro: Most endpoints used by these integrations are authenticated. You have two ways to satisfy that requirement.
auth.optAtitle: Option A — API token (recommended for integrations)
auth.optAbody1: Open the dashboard and go to Settings → Security → API Tokens. Click Generate token, give it a name (e.g. homepage, home-assistant, prometheus), and copy the token — it's shown once. Long-lived (one-year expiry by default), individually revocable, and what you should be using for any non-browser client.
auth.optAbody2: From that point every request is just:
auth.optBbody: Useful for scripts that authenticate as a human user. The returned token is short-lived; most integrations should prefer Option A.
auth.outro: The TOTP field is only required when 2FA is enabled on the account. Token rotation, revocation, password policy and the audit log live in <link>Access & Authentication</link>.
auth.httpsIntro: Every recipe below uses http:// in the URLs to keep the examples short. If you've enabled TLS on the Monitor (Settings → Security → SSL/HTTPS), swap http:// for https:// in every URL — that's the only change. Two notes specific to certain tools:
httpsItems: Self-signed certificates. Home Assistant's rest: integration verifies TLS by default. If the Monitor is using its own self-signed cert, add verify_ssl: false to each REST block (alongside scan_interval:), or import the Monitor's CA into HA's trust store. Same for any tool that refuses untrusted certs.
Prometheus already has scheme: https ready in the scrape config below; uncomment / leave it as https if TLS is enabled on the Monitor.

homepage.heading: Homepage
homepage.intro: Homepage is a fully static, customizable application dashboard. ProxMenux Monitor plugs into it via the built-in customapi widget — paste a service entry into services.yaml, restart Homepage, and the card appears with live numbers.
homepage.iconCalloutTitle: The official ProxMenux logo is on dashboardicons.com
homepage.iconCalloutBody: The recipes below use icon: proxmenux.png. Homepage automatically resolves bare filenames against dashboardicons.com — a curated icon library for self-hosted dashboards. The ProxMenux entry lives at dashboardicons.com/icons/external/proxmenux and Homepage pulls it on first render. Same lookup works for thousands of other tools (Telegram, Discord, Grafana, Tailscale, etc.) — just write icon: <name>.png in any service entry.
homepage.imageAlt: Homepage dashboard showing three ProxMenux Monitor cards (EDGE, VOID, DREAM) with uptime, CPU, RAM and temperature for each Proxmox host
homepage.imageCaption: Three ProxMenux Monitor instances rendered as Homepage cards — uptime, CPU, RAM and CPU temperature read live from /api/system on each host every 10 s.
homepage.basicIntro: Use this when ProxMenux Monitor is on a trusted network and you haven't enabled authentication on the Monitor side yet. The simplest possible services.yaml entry:
homepage.authedIntro: Generate an API token in Settings → Security → API Tokens on the Monitor, copy it, and paste it into the Authorization header below — replace the example token shown after Bearer with the one you just copied:
homepage.authedOutro: Restart Homepage and the card lights up with live values. Reuse the same token across all Homepage widgets pointing at the same ProxMenux Monitor host.
homepage.multiIntro: For a richer view, render three separate cards backed by different endpoints — one for system metrics, one for storage, one for network. Use the same token in every card; it's the same Monitor instance.
homepage.multiCalloutBody: Repeat the entry block for each host to get the multi-card layout shown above. Each entry uses the URL http://<host>:8008 of that host’s Monitor instance. Generate and store a token for each host; separate installations have their own signing secrets, so a token from one host should not be assumed to work on another.

homeAssistant.heading: Home Assistant
homeAssistant.intro: These examples use Home Assistant’s built-in rest integration, so a custom HACS component is not required. It reads Monitor endpoints described in the API Reference and turns their responses into sensors and attributes for automations. The reference configuration below provides roughly 25 sensors for system resources, health, VMs/CTs, storage, network and ProxMenux updates. Add it to configuration.yaml and reload or restart HA.
homeAssistant.imageAlt: Home Assistant dashboard showing ProxMenux Monitor entities — health status badge, CPU / RAM / Temp gauges, VM count, storage usage and active errors counter
homeAssistant.imageCaption: ProxMenux Monitor as a first-class Home Assistant integration — sensors built from the YAML recipe below.
homeAssistant.step1Body: Store the token in Home Assistant’s secrets.yaml to keep it separate from the main configuration. Include the full Bearer prefix and token in one value so YAML can reference it as a header. This file is not encrypted and must also be kept private. Its location depends on the installation, typically /config/secrets.yaml on HA OS or Container.
homeAssistant.step2Body: Six REST blocks cover the full surface — one per major Monitor area. Each block has a sensible scan_interval tuned to how often the underlying data changes (system resources every 30 s, health every 60 s, slowly-changing inventories every 5-10 min). Paste into configuration.yaml:
homeAssistant.step3Title: 3 · Add binary sensors and template helpers
homeAssistant.step3Body: Two binary sensors and a couple of template sensors round out the integration — they make automations and Lovelace conditional cards much cleaner than chaining Jinja in every place.
homeAssistant.step4Body: From the HA UI: Developer Tools → YAML → Check Configuration first to validate the syntax, then All YAML configuration reload (or full restart). After it comes back, filter Settings → Devices & Services → Entities by proxmenux — you should see all ~25 entities populating within one scan interval.
homeAssistant.replaceTitle: Replacing an earlier version of this recipe?
homeAssistant.replaceBody: If you tried a previous version of these YAML blocks, Home Assistant's entity registry may have cached the old entity IDs and stale entities will still appear (with Entidad no encontrada warnings in your Lovelace cards). Clean state in two steps: delete the previous rest: and template: blocks from configuration.yaml, reload, and then under Settings → Devices & Services → Entities filter by proxmenux and remove any entries marked "Restored" or showing as unavailable. Then paste the current YAML and reload again — the new entities register cleanly.
homeAssistant.step5Body: The YAML below is a single vertical-stack card that combines all the sub-cards in one block — header with logo, quick KPIs, system detail, VMs, storage, network and a conditional health-issues card. To use it: open your dashboard, click the pencil (edit), click Add card, scroll to the bottom and pick Manual, then paste:
homeAssistant.viewTipTitle: Want it as a full dashboard view instead of a single card?
homeAssistant.viewTipBody: Open the dashboard's 3-dot menu → Raw configuration editor and add a new view with this header (above the cards: list from the YAML above):
homeAssistant.viewTipOutro: That gives you a dedicated tab/view in your dashboard with its own icon and title, instead of one long card on an existing view.
homeAssistant.altViewIntro: To create a dedicated view tab inside an existing dashboard, rather than one card within another view, add a view with the YAML below. A view is a tab within a dashboard; it does not create a new sidebar dashboard entry. Steps:
altViewSteps: Open the dashboard where you want the new tab.
Click the pencil (edit dashboard) at the top right.
Click the + tab at the end of the existing tabs to create a new view.
In the dialog that opens, switch to the Code editor tab (top right of the dialog — toggles between visual editor and YAML).
Save. The new ProxMenux Monitor view appears as a tab inside the dashboard with its cards.
homeAssistant.twoEditorsTitle: Two YAML editors in HA — pick the right one
homeAssistant.twoEditorsIntro: Home Assistant has two YAML editors that look similar but expect different formats:
twoEditorsItems: Single-view editor (this recipe) — opened from the + tab or from Edit view → Code editor. Expects the body of one view directly: title:, path:, cards: at the top level, no leading dash.
Whole-dashboard Raw editor — opened from the dashboard's 3-dot menu. Expects the entire views: list, with each view as a list item (leading -).
homeAssistant.twoEditorsOutro: Pasting view-body YAML into the whole-dashboard editor (or vice versa) leaves you with a Vista sin nombre and cards: []. The YAML below is for the single-view editor — paste exactly as shown.
homeAssistant.viewImageAlt: Home Assistant dedicated view rendering ProxMenux Monitor — picture-entity header, glance KPIs, and System / VMs / Storage / Network entity cards laid out automatically by HA across multiple columns
homeAssistant.viewImageCaption: The dedicated ProxMenux Monitor view on a wide screen. A Masonry layout arranges the cards into columns automatically; the layout depends on the configured view type.
homeAssistant.twoColTipTitle: Want a fixed two-column layout instead of the auto layout?
homeAssistant.twoColTipBody: Replace any pair of cards (e.g. System + VMs, or Storage + Network) with a single horizontal-stack wrapping both, so they always render side by side regardless of screen width:
homeAssistant.twoColTipOutro: On mobile the row stays compressed; HA's auto layout (no horizontal-stack) reflows better at narrow widths.

homeAssistant.logoBody: The picture-entity card at the top of the Lovelace YAML pulls the official ProxMenux logo from <a1>dashboardicons.com</a1> — a free icon library curated for self-hosted dashboards. The ProxMenux entry lives at <a2>dashboardicons.com/icons/external/proxmenux</a2>. Home Assistant fetches the SVG over HTTPS on first render and caches it.
homeAssistant.logoBrokenTitle: If the logo card shows a broken image
homeAssistant.logoBrokenIntro: Some HA installs (firewalled networks, content blockers, hosts without public internet) can't reach jsdelivr.net at render time. The fix is a local copy:
logoBrokenSteps: Save it to /config/www/icons/proxmenux.svg on your HA host.
In the Lovelace YAML, replace the image: URL with /local/icons/proxmenux.svg. Save and reload — the image renders from the local file, no internet needed.
homeAssistant.scanTipBody: Polling /api/system every 30 s is a reasonable starting point. /api/health/full normally reads a background result valid for up to 6 min; polling every 60 s does not bypass that cache. Try 5 min for /api/storage/summary and an hour for /api/proxmenux/update-status. Adjust intervals for your hardware and number of hosts.

grafana.heading: Prometheus + Grafana
grafana.intro: ProxMenux Monitor exposes GET /api/prometheus, returning Prometheus text exposition format 0.0.4. It requires a bearer token when Monitor authentication is enabled. Configure Prometheus to collect it, then use Grafana to visualize the metrics in your time-series database.
grafana.imageAlt: Grafana dashboard rendering ProxMenux Monitor metrics — CPU usage gauge, memory usage timeseries, running VMs count, network throughput
grafana.imageCaption: A basic Grafana dashboard built from the ProxMenux Prometheus scrape — CPU, memory, running VMs, network throughput. The full metric catalogue lives in the <link>API Reference → Prometheus metrics</link>.
grafana.step1Title: 1 · Add the scrape job to Prometheus
grafana.step1Body: Pass the API token via Prometheus' native authorization block (cleaner than custom headers and works with secret stores):
grafana.step1After: Reload Prometheus with kill -HUP <PID> (replace PID with the Prometheus process ID), systemctl reload prometheus if supported by your service, or docker compose restart prometheus for a container. Check Status → Targets: the proxmenux job should become UP within one collection interval. Monitor metrics carry a node="<hostname>" label to distinguish hosts.
grafana.tokenTipTitle: Keep the token in a separate file
grafana.tokenTipBody: For production deployments avoid inlining the token. Prometheus supports credentials_file: /etc/prometheus/secrets/proxmenux.token as an alternative — keep the token in a 0600 file and let Prometheus read it.
grafana.step2Title: 2 · Verify the scrape with a couple of queries
grafana.step2Body: Before configuring Grafana, confirm Prometheus actually has the data. Open Prometheus' own UI at http://<prometheus-host>:9090, click Query and run any of these — you should get back live numbers from your Proxmox host:

verifyRows.confirms: Returns 1 if Prometheus is successfully scraping the Monitor, 0 if not. The fastest sanity check.
Current CPU usage % of the Proxmox host. Should change if you refresh the query a few seconds apart.
Number of running guests. Compare against what you see in the Proxmox UI.
Host uptime in days. Should match the value you'd see in uptime on the Proxmox shell.

grafana.calloutTitle: The 401 you may see when clicking the endpoint URL is fine
grafana.calloutBody: With Monitor authentication enabled, clicking the endpoint link on Status → Targets fetches /api/prometheus in the browser without Prometheus’s bearer header. The response can contain '{'"error":"Authentication required"'}'. Check the target’s actual State: UP to confirm that Prometheus itself is collecting successfully with its configured token.
grafana.step3Title: 3 · Add Prometheus as a Grafana data source
grafana.step3Body: In Grafana, open Connections → Data sources → Add new → Prometheus. Set the Prometheus URL, for example http://prometheus.lan:9090, then save and test. If your Prometheus server requires authentication, configure that separately here. The Monitor API token belongs in the Prometheus collection job.
grafana.step4Title: 4 · Build panels with these PromQL queries
grafana.step4Body: A starter set that maps directly to what users typically watch on a Proxmox host:
grafana.outro: Add each query as a Grafana panel, set the right visualization (Stat for gauges, Time series for trends), and group panels into rows by category. Use the node label as a dashboard variable (Settings → Variables → New → Query → label_values(proxmox_cpu_usage, node)) to filter all panels by host.

uptimeKuma.heading: Uptime Kuma and other status checkers
uptimeKuma.intro: For a keyword-based check, use GET /api/system-info. This route has no token decorator and returns hostname, uptime and a health status mapped to healthy, warning or critical. It is a public probe, unlike the authenticated detailed health endpoints.
kumaSteps: In Uptime Kuma, click + Add New Monitor.
Keyword: healthy (the value of health.status when the host is OK).
Save. This system-info route does not require a bearer header.
uptimeKuma.healthchecksBody: A cron job can query /api/system-info and test .health.status == "healthy". Only after a successful health test should it send a success ping to the check’s unique Healthchecks.io URL. Healthchecks.io receives pings from jobs; it does not poll the Monitor URL. An HTTP 2xx response alone does not prove that the reported host health is good.
uptimeKuma.richBody: For the full state — ten health categories, active errors and dismissed items — use GET /api/health/full. It returns the dashboard modal’s data in one response and needs a bearer token when Monitor authentication is enabled.

workflows.heading: n8n, Zapier and custom scripts
workflows.intro: Workflow tools and scripts can send notifications through a POST to /api/notifications/send, for example after a CI failure or an overlong cron job. This is a direct send: it bypasses the event queue and fingerprint cooldown. It still uses channel formatting, optional AI rewriting and delivery to configured channels. Apply any required duplicate control in the caller.
workflows.n8nBody: In n8n, use an HTTP Request node with POST, the URL above and the same JSON body as curl. Choose generic Header Auth credentials: set the header name to Authorization and its value to Bearer YOUR_API_TOKEN, replacing the placeholder. Connect a schedule, webhook or other preceding node to trigger the request.
workflows.severityBody: Severity values are INFO, WARNING or CRITICAL in uppercase. The data object supplies event context and template fields. On this endpoint, AI rewriting receives only the title and message; fields in data are not sent to the provider. See Notifications → Event catalogue for event semantics.

pveWebhook.heading: Native Proxmox VE webhook (inbound)
pveWebhook.intro1: The PVE notification system was introduced in 8.1; native webhook targets require Proxmox VE 8.3 or later. Enabling notifications with Enable Notifications in Settings attempts to register the Monitor as a target. PVE notifications routed to that target, such as backup or replication reports, then enter the Monitor’s dispatch flow. Setup depends on the notification configuration being writable and available.
pveWebhook.intro2: Mechanics, the body template PVE sends, the entries written to /etc/pve/notifications.cfg, and behaviour in clusters are documented in Notifications → PVE webhook integration.
